workflow_title: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing of clinical bacterial isolates: broth microdilution MIC determination, quality control and EUCAST clinical breakpoint interpretation
occupation_scope: Clinical microbiologist; medical laboratory scientist; antimicrobial stewardship pharmacist
workflow_summary: A clinical microbiology unit determines minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) for bacterial isolates by broth microdilution, runs EUCAST quality-control strains and internal QC, then interprets results against the current EUCAST clinical breakpoint tables to report isolates as susceptible, susceptible with increased exposure or resistant for patient therapy guidance.
source_reference: Primary: EUCAST MIC determination page read in full, fetched HTTP 200 (https://www.eucast.org/bacteria/methodology-and-instructions/mic-determination/): states EUCAST MIC determination for non-fastidious organisms is 'in complete agreement' with ISO; fastidious organisms use MH-F broth (MH plus lysed horse blood plus beta-NAD); hosts the EUCAST recommendation for broth microdilution MIC determination and the EUCAST reading guide for broth microdilution v5.0 (January 2024); QC tables v16.0 valid from 1 January 2026 for routine and extended internal QC. Supporting: EUCAST clinical breakpoint tables page cited directly by the fetched page (https://www.eucast.org/bacteria/clinical-breakpoints-and-interpretation/clinical-breakpoint-tables/, not fetched separately this session); ISO 20776-1:2019 and ISO 20776-2:2021 referenced on the fetched page (metadata-level verification only, standard texts are paywalled).
expert_raw_materials: Pure culture of the clinical isolate; Mueller-Hinton or MH-F broth and MIC panels; EUCAST MIC method and reading-guide documents; EUCAST QC tables v16.0 and clinical breakpoint tables; QC reference strains; laboratory information system with isolate and patient metadata
usage_permissions: EUCAST documents and tables are issued by EUCAST/ESCMID for free professional use (E1 https://www.eucast.org/bacteria/methodology-and-instructions/mic-determination/); ISO 20776 parts are fee-based ISO standards; the laboratory runs under its quality-management system and accreditation scope (ISO 15189 for medical laboratories)
task_input: Purified bacterial isolate from a patient or surveillance sample plus request metadata such as specimen type, patient context and the antibiotics to be tested
professional_operations: Prepare a 0.5 McFarland inoculum of the pure isolate in the appropriate broth; inoculate the MIC panel covering the requested antibiotics; incubate under the conditions EUCAST specifies for the organism group; read endpoints following the EUCAST reading guide; run EUCAST routine and internal QC strains and record results against the QC tables; interpret each MIC with the current EUCAST clinical breakpoint table and S/I/R definitions; re-test or escalate when QC is out of range or endpoints are unreadable
expected_deliverable: A QC-validated susceptibility report assigning susceptible, susceptible with increased exposure or resistant per antibiotic, released to the treating clinician through the laboratory information system
success_criteria: QC strain MICs inside the EUCAST QC table ranges on the day of testing; readable, interpretable endpoints; report consistent with the EUCAST breakpoint table version the laboratory has adopted
verification_approach: Daily cross-check of QC strain values against EUCAST QC tables v16.0; second reader or electronic endpoint reading for ambiguous panels; periodic external quality assessment schemes; laboratory MIC distributions compared with EUCAST reference distributions
platform_dependencies: BSL-2-capable clinical microbiology laboratory; temperature-controlled incubator; calibrated commercial or in-house MIC panels and broths; EUCAST documents and annual tables; laboratory information system; trained technical and medical staff
blocking_risks: Wet-laboratory steps and biosafety containment cannot be replaced by software; commercial MIC panel supply chains; the ISO reference-method texts are paywalled so only metadata-level verification was possible here; breakpoint tables change annually so any automated interpreter must be re-validated against each year's version
expert_capability: Clinical microbiology training; endpoint reading skill; knowledge of EUCAST breakpoints, intrinsic-resistance rules and organism-specific exceptions; laboratory QC management
cross_domain_overlap: Adjacent to S1-02A engineering instrumentation rows that measure chemicals, since only the clinical isolate susceptibility interpretation with the EUCAST standard defines this workflow; no A-round duplicate carries the clinical AST workflow
granularity_check: Right granularity: a bounded laboratory workflow repeated daily per isolate batch, complete from inoculum to clinical report
pending_confirmation: Confirm with EUCAST that the two PDF documents listed on the fetched page are the current versions at merge time and that the breakpoint-table URL resolves for the coordinator environment; the page itself was fetched and verified, PDF bodies were not downloaded
data_usage_authorization: Clinical isolates and patient metadata are processed under the laboratory accreditation and quality-management scope; EUCAST documents are freely available for professional use (E1 https://www.eucast.org/bacteria/methodology-and-instructions/mic-determination/); ISO 20776-1:2019 and ISO 20776-2:2021 are fee-based ISO publications referenced by the primary
privacy_considerations: Patient-linked susceptibility records are health data; in the EU the GDPR treats health and genetic data as special-category personal data (Art 4(13), 4(15), Art 9) and pseudonymised isolate records remain personal data unless truly anonymised (Art 4(1), Recital 26) (E1 https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/); in the US HIPAA-covered laboratories protect patient microbiology results as protected health information; routine reports are therefore pseudonymised
research_ethics: Routine clinical susceptibility testing is diagnostic care, not research; any research or surveillance reuse of isolates requires institutional ethics review and, for human-derived material, consent per the Declaration of Helsinki paragraphs 23 and 32 (E1 https://www.wma.net/policies-post/wma-declaration-of-helsinki/); aggregated surveillance reporting follows national and EUCAST statistical protocols
reproducibility_assessment: The reference method is anchored to ISO 20776-1:2019 so MICs are comparable across laboratories; EUCAST publishes annual QC ranges and breakpoint tables, making the interpretive layer fully reproducible (E1 https://www.eucast.org/bacteria/methodology-and-instructions/mic-determination/); the physical pipetting and read-out steps are the operator-dependent part and are controlled by QC strains rather than software
primary_claim: The fetched EUCAST page documents the whole professional workflow: a MIC determination method harmonised with ISO 20776, fastidious-organism media rules, a reading guide, QC tables and breakpoint interpretation as the daily clinical microbiology standard
engineering_pending: YES: tool runs only under a condition (Windows GUI, third-party container, or registration); Linux path NOT verified

workflow_title: Genome-scale metabolic network reconstruction with manual curation, confidence scoring and MEMOTE quality control
occupation_scope: Systems biologist; metabolic modeler; computational microbiologist; industrial biotechnologist
workflow_summary: A metabolic modeler drafts a genome-scale metabolic reconstruction from genome annotation and biochemical databases, refines it manually against literature, thermodynamic and localization rules, converts it to SBML, and iteratively evaluates it with biomass-precursor and phenotype tests plus the MEMOTE test suite until the model reproduces observed phenotypes.
source_reference: Primary: Thiele and Palsson protocol read in full through Step 22 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3125167/, Nat Protoc 5(1):93-121, 2010, DOI 10.1038/nprot.2009.203): a 5-stage protocol from draft reconstruction through manual refinement, conversion, network evaluation and prospective use, with confidence scoring 0-4, mass/charge balancing, directionality rules, GPR association rules, and QC/QA tests of biomass precursors and secretions. Supporting: MEMOTE consortium letter read in full (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7082222/, Nat Biotechnol 38(3):272-276, 2020, DOI 10.1038/s41587-020-0446-y): community-standard test suite in four areas (annotation, basic tests, biomass reaction, stoichiometry), snapshot/diff/history reports, continuous integration on GitHub/GitLab, validated on 10,780 models from 7 collections, and reporting about 70 percent of manually published GEMs have at least one stoichiometrically unbalanced metabolite
expert_raw_materials: Latest genome annotation of the target organism; biochemical databases (KEGG, BRENDA, SEED, EcoCyc, PubChem, TCDB per the protocol Table 1); literature on verified metabolic functions; physiological data for growth conditions; SBML tooling
usage_permissions: The biomolecular databases consumed carry their own terms (KEGG and BRENDA academic/commercial licenses, not re-verified this session); the protocol article is freely readable from PMC (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3125167/); finished models can be released under CC0 on BioModels (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383975/)
task_input: An annotated genome plus the curation objective, such as growth-yield prediction, gene-knockout phenotyping or strain-design for a target organism
professional_operations: Draft the reconstruction from automated annotation of metabolic functions; verify each reaction against literature, phylogeny and organism-specific substrate/cofactor usage; compute charged formulas at intracellular pH; balance mass and charge; assign directionality from thermodynamics and rules of thumb; localize compartments; build gene-protein-reaction associations; apply 0-4 confidence scores; convert to SBML; evaluate with biomass-precursor and secretion tests; run MEMOTE and fix annotation or stoichiometry failures; iterate until phenotype predictions match experiments
expected_deliverable: A reviewed, SBML3FBC-encoded genome-scale metabolic model with MIRIAM-compliant annotations, confidence scores and a passing MEMOTE report, published with the reconstruction study
success_criteria: All reactions mass and charge balanced with organism-appropriate directionality; biomass-precursor production test passes under the selected growth conditions; MEMOTE report shows no unannotated or inconsistent components above the project thresholds
verification_approach: MEMOTE snapshot, diff and history reports across versions; reproduction of experimental growth phenotypes and gene-knockout predictions; cross-checks against physiological data for the organism
platform_dependencies: Spreadsheet ledger for curation; an SBML editor or libSBML tooling; the protocol's MATLAB COBRA Toolbox stage replaced in current practice by open Python tooling such as cobrapy; MEMOTE as open-source Python; Git-based version control for continuous integration
blocking_risks: Manual curation is expert-labour-bound, documented at about 6 months for a medium-sized bacterium and up to 2 years with 6 people for human reconstructions; KEGG/BRENDA license terms restrict bulk commercial reuse; stoichiometric balancing and pathway directionality need literature review that resists automation
expert_capability: Biochemistry and microbial physiology knowledge; familiarity with GPR associations, thermodynamics of reactions and constraint-based modeling; software skills for SBML tooling and version control
cross_domain_overlap: Overlaps biomolecular workflows when kinetic or structural detail enters reactions, and genomics workflows which provide the annotation input; distinct from BioModels curation (life_sysmic_wf03) which curates a submitted model instead of building one; no A-round duplicate
granularity_check: Right granularity: one reconstruction project of weeks to months bounded by the protocol's five stages and closed by MEMOTE testing
pending_confirmation: Protocol read through Step 22 only, later stages verified at section-heading level, so confirm the remaining steps against the published protocol; verify the cobrapy license and current KEGG/BRENDA reuse terms with the respective providers
data_usage_authorization: Reconstruction consumes public database content (KEGG, BRENDA, SEED, EcoCyc, PubChem, TCDB listed in the protocol Table 1) each under its own terms; the protocol article is free to read via PMC (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3125167/); released models can be placed under CC0 at BioModels (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383975/)
privacy_considerations: Microbial reconstructions contain no personal data; human genome-scale models built from literature and published datasets are not individually identifying, but a model validated against patient-derived omics would inherit the status of those data, so GDPR Art 4(1) and 4(13) apply in the EU (E1 https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/)
research_ethics: No human or animal subjects at the model level; any human omics used for validation require the ethics approvals of the source studies per Helsinki paragraphs 23 and 32 (E1 https://www.wma.net/policies-post/wma-declaration-of-helsinki/); pathogen-targeted metabolic modeling raises dual-use review questions that funders and institutions screen
reproducibility_assessment: SBML3FBC encoding plus MIRIAM-compliant annotations support exchange and re-simulation, and MEMOTE history reports record every tested edit, which is the workflow's reproducibility backbone (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7082222/)
primary_claim: The protocol documents the whole genome-scale metabolic reconstruction workflow as practiced, from genome annotation through manual refinement and QC/QA testing to prospective use, with explicit confidence scoring and thermodynamic checks
engineering_pending: YES: open-source substitute covers part of the proprietary tool; functional equivalence NOT verified

workflow_title: Curation and deposition of a biochemical model to BioModels with MIRIAM-compliant annotation
occupation_scope: Systems biologist; metabolic modeler; computational microbiologist; model curator
workflow_summary: A modeler prepares an SBML model with database cross-references and ontology annotations, submits it to EMBL-EBI BioModels, and works with curators who annotate components and verify that simulations reproduce the published results, releasing a curated model with a curation figure.
source_reference: Primary: Chelliah et al. read in full (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383975/, Nucleic Acids Res 43:D542-D548, 2015, DOI 10.1093/nar/gku1181): documents the submission-to-curation workflow, including unique model identifiers citable in articles, advance reviewer access, publisher recommendation from EMBO press, PLoS, RSC, BMC, ScienceDirect and FEBS, a two-phase annotation step (Identifiers.org cross-references, MIRIAM compliance evaluation) followed by curation focused on reproducibility of published simulation results with a curation figure attached, and the split between curated and non-curated models. Supporting: Glont et al. 2018 (PMID 29126160, PMCID PMC5753244) records the version-control-backed curation infrastructure; Juty et al. 2015 (PMCID PMC4360671) is a repository use tutorial; Li et al. 2010 (PMCID PMC2909940) states models are freely distributed and the infrastructure is GPL; all three verified at metadata level via Europe PMC REST
expert_raw_materials: The finished SBML or CellML model file; simulation scripts able to reproduce the published figures; citations to the source publication; database identifiers and ontology terms for all model components (ChEBI, GO, taxonomy)
usage_permissions: Repository content license verified from the primary: BioModels content is provided under the Creative Commons CC0 Public Domain Dedication, so all models may be freely downloaded, used, modified and redistributed by any user (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4383975/)
task_input: A model accompanied by its publication and the simulation protocol used to generate the published results
professional_operations: Submit the model to BioModels and obtain the unique model identifier; supply cross-references for components; curators annotate against external databases and ontology terms via Identifiers.org and evaluate MIRIAM compliance; curators attempt to reproduce the published simulation results; if reproduction fails, authors are contacted and revisions requested; for reproducible models a curation figure with representative simulation results and curator comments on the protocol is attached; the model is released as curated or non-curated
expected_deliverable: A curated BioModels entry with MIRIAM-compliant annotation, a curation figure, a stable identifier citable in the associated publication, and public CC0 availability
success_criteria: Curators can reproduce the published simulation results from the deposited files; all components carry resolvable identifiers; the entry is promoted to curated status

workflow_title: Reproducible microbiome community analysis from amplicon reads with QIIME 2 provenance-tracked workflows

workflow_summary: A microbiome analyst imports multiplexed amplicon reads, demultiplexes and quality-controls them, builds a sequence-variant feature table through denoising, computes phylogenetic alpha and beta diversity, assigns taxonomy and runs statistical tests, producing interactive visualizations whose full data provenance is recorded automatically.
source_reference: Primary: Bolyen et al. read in full (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7015180/, Nat Biotechnol 37(8):852-857, 2019, DOI 10.1038/s41587-019-0209-9): the QIIME 2 platform announcement with plugin architecture, DADA2/Deblur QC plugins, taxonomy assignment, phylogenetic insertion, paired-sample, time-series and machine-learning plugins, automatic data-provenance tracking with corrupted-result detection, semantic typing of results, Jupyter Notebook and CWL workflow support, and four worked examples including a 37,680-sample UniFrac principal coordinate analysis; the letter states QIIME 2 is BSD 3-clause licensed and free for all use including commercial. Supporting: the official Moving Pictures tutorial fetched HTTP 200 (https://docs.qiime2.org/2024.10/tutorials/moving-pictures/): the stepwise canonical workflow from import through demultiplexing, DADA2 or Deblur denoising, feature-table summaries, phylogenetic tree construction, core diversity metrics (Shannon, Faith PD, Bray-Curtis, Jaccard, UniFrac), group significance tests, Emperor ordination, Greengenes classifier taxonomy assignment, taxon bar plots and ANCOM-BC differential abundance; the page states the 2024.10 docs are superseded by amplicon-docs.qiime2.org as of the 2025.4 release
expert_raw_materials: Demultiplexed or multiplexed FASTQ files with barcode metadata; sample metadata table; a pre-trained or self-trained taxonomy classifier (Greengenes 13_8 or SILVA classifiers); reference phylogeny for UniFrac metrics
usage_permissions: QIIME 2 is open source under a BSD 3-clause license and free for all use including commercial (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7015180/); input sequences are typically stored in SRA/ENA under their submission policies (E1 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/home/about/policies/); pre-trained classifier artifacts carry their own database terms, such as SILVA academic-use conditions, not re-verified this session
task_input: Multiplexed marker-gene amplicon reads plus a sample metadata table that defines the groups and time points of interest
professional_operations: Import reads as a QIIME 2 artifact with the correct semantic type; demultiplex with barcode metadata and summarize sequence quality; choose trim and truncation parameters from the quality plots; run DADA2 or Deblur denoising to obtain a FeatureTable and representative sequences; summarize feature and sample frequencies; generate a phylogenetic tree; compute core alpha and beta diversity metrics with an even sampling depth; run group-significance tests (including PERMANOVA); assign taxonomy with the q2-feature-classifier plugin; produce taxon bar plots and ordination plots; optionally run ANCOM-BC differential abundance; archive artifacts with their recorded provenance
expected_deliverable: A provenance-tracked set of QIIME 2 artifacts and interactive visualizations plus a methods description sufficient to re-run or inspect every analysis step
success_criteria: Demultiplexing and denoising summaries show expected per-sample depth and quality; diversity estimates respond to chosen sampling depth without obvious rarefaction artefacts; every artifact carries an intact provenance graph that QIIME 2 accepts
verification_approach: Interactive quality plots checked between steps; alpha-rarefaction plateau inspection for sequencing sufficiency; provenance graphs opened in QIIME 2 View to audit the analysis chain; corrupted-result detection flags broken provenance
platform_dependencies: A Linux or macOS environment with QIIME 2 installed via conda; adequate RAM for denoising; optional GPU or cluster scaling of heavy steps; QIIME 2 View or local tools for visualizations
blocking_risks: Classifier database license terms restrict some commercial uses; the analyst must pin classifier and software versions to guarantee reproducibility; the platform letter itself is not a step protocol, so the canonical workflow is assembled from the letter plus the official tutorial
expert_capability: Microbiome data analysis skill; quality-plot interpretation for parameter choice; understanding of rarefaction, diversity metrics and compositionality caveats; command-line and notebook fluency
cross_domain_overlap: Consumes genomics read-processing ideas but its objects are community diversity and composition; adjacent to STORMS reporting (life_sysmic_wf05) which specifies how this analysis is written up; distinct from the A-round outbreak investigation (med_pubhealth_wf02) because this is research data science, not case response
granularity_check: Right granularity: one analysis campaign from raw reads to archived, provenance-tracked deliverables
pending_confirmation: Primary is a platform letter rather than a step protocol, so this row is agent_inferred_combination combining it with the official tutorial; confirm with the QIIME 2 development team (forum.qiime2.org) that the import-demultiplex-denoise-diversity-taxonomy chain is the accepted community default, which would support an upgrade to industry_standard_complete

workflow_title: Application of the STORMS checklist to report a human microbiome study for publication
occupation_scope: Microbiome bioinformatician; microbial ecologist; clinical microbiome researcher; journal reviewer; scientific editor
workflow_summary: An author or reviewer works through the 17-section STORMS checklist, built on STROBE, to verify that a human microbiome manuscript reports study design, laboratory and sequencing methods, bioinformatic and statistical methods, reproducibility items and data availability before submission or review.
source_reference: Primary: Mirzayi et al. read in full (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9105086/, Nat Med 27(11):1885-1892, 2021, DOI 10.1038/s41591-021-01552-x): the Genomic Standards Consortium and Massive Analysis and Quality Control Society checklist with sections from abstract items 1.0-1.3, methods for participants 3.0-3.9, laboratory methods 4.0-4.17, data sources 5.0, causal-inference considerations 6.0-6.1, bioinformatics and statistics 7.0-7.9, reproducible research 8.0-8.5, results 9.0-10.4, discussion 11.0-14.0 and other information 15.0-17.0; it recommends depositing raw and processed data in NCBI or EMBL-EBI repositories and using Zenodo or Publisso for processed-data DOIs, and it provides a public-domain checklist template at https://stormsmicrobiome.org
expert_raw_materials: The draft manuscript; the STORMS checklist and the STROBE guideline on which it builds; laboratory and software version records; data-access statements
usage_permissions: The STORMS checklist is a public-domain reporting standard with a template reusable at https://stormsmicrobiome.org (cited by the primary); the article itself is readable via PMC (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9105086/)
task_input: A complete human microbiome study manuscript plus its methods, results and data-availability records
professional_operations: Check the abstract reports study design, sequencing method and body sites (items 1.x); verify the introduction states hypotheses or pre-registered objectives (2.x); check participant eligibility, covariates and antibiotic exposure are reported (3.x); verify laboratory methods from collection through extraction, controls and sequencing strategy (4.x); confirm data transformations, QC, statistical methods and software versions are disclosed (7.x); confirm raw and processed data deposition or justified access restrictions (8.x); verify outcome reporting includes descriptive microbiome analyses, differential abundance magnitudes and null results (10.x); return a completed checklist with the review
expected_deliverable: A STORMS-completed checklist accompanying the manuscript, with any unmet items corrected in the manuscript before submission or acceptance
success_criteria: Every applicable checklist item is addressable with a manuscript location or data-access statement; deposition records exist for raw and processed data where possible
verification_approach: Cross-check each checklist item against the manuscript text and the public repositories named in the data-availability statement (NCBI, EMBL-EBI, Zenodo, Publisso)
platform_dependencies: No software is required beyond document tooling and repository web interfaces; the checklist exists as a printable and editable form
blocking_risks: Restricted-access human data cannot always be deposited openly, so items 8.x verification depends on honest access statements; harmful-to-generalize practices are not automatically caught by a checklist
expert_capability: Microbiome study-design and analysis knowledge needed to judge whether reported methods satisfy each item; familiarity with STROBE on which STORMS builds
cross_domain_overlap: Reporting layer for the analysis workflow in life_sysmic_wf04 and for genomics rows that feed microbiome studies; parallel to the MIFlowCyt reporting workflow (life_cellimg_wf01) but specialized to microbiome studies; distinct from the A-round CDC outbreak investigation (med_pubhealth_wf02) which is a response workflow, not a reporting standard
granularity_check: Right granularity: a bounded per-manuscript reporting and verification task, complete from draft to checklist-signed submission
pending_confirmation: Confirm with the Genomic Standards Consortium and MAQC Society that STORMS remains the current human microbiome reporting standard and whether a revision is planned; the checklist template URL was cited by the primary but not fetched this session
data_usage_authorization: Checklist items 8.0-8.5 require stating where raw and processed data reside, recommend NCBI/EMBL-EBI repositories plus Zenodo or Publisso DOIs for processed data, and require describing any protected information and its access route (E1 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9105086/)
privacy_considerations: Item 8.0 requires describing protected information and how such data can be accessed; human microbiome data can identify individuals and are genetic/health data under GDPR Art 4(13), 4(15) and Art 9 in the EU (E1 https://gdpr-info.eu/art-4-gdpr/) and under NIH GDS Policy for large-scale US studies (E1 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/home/about/policies/)

primary_claim: The STORMS paper documents, item by item, the complete reporting workflow for human microbiome studies as a community checklist for authors and peer reviewers

verification_approach: MQSA facility audits and medical outcome audits; double reading where adopted by the program; correlation of BI-RADS 4 and 5 with pathology; peer review of discordant cases

blocking_risks: Reading requires FDA-certified display systems and institutional PHI access; the lay-letter and 7-day communication rules are mandatory MQSA compliance obligations; interpretation depends on certified radiologist judgment, and the PACS workstation is an interactive non-Linux institutional GUI, so the workflow needs a task redesign before any Linux-based automation

workflow_title: Clinical decision support (CDS) selection, implementation, and lifecycle monitoring for health IT-enabled clinical workflows

workflow_summary: An institution reviews a clinical problem (care gap, alert fatigue, safety event), selects or designs a CDS intervention using the Five Rights model, implements it in the EHR, then evaluates impact, monitors ongoing performance, and updates or retires it under institutional governance.
source_reference: PRIMARY: Petersen et al., 'Recommendations for the safe, effective use of adaptive CDS in the US healthcare system', AMIA position paper, JAMIA 2021;28(4):677-684, doi 10.1093/jamia/ocaa319, full text fetched at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7973467/ - documents the complete CDS lifecycle stages (design and development, implementation, evaluation, ongoing monitoring and maintenance) with transparency metrics, assurance cases, performance indicators, institutional review groups, and workforce education. SUPPORTING: eCQI Resource Center CDS page (https://ecqi.healthit.gov/cds, fetched) - CMS definition of CDS, the CDS Five Rights model (right information, people, format, channel, time) from Improving Outcomes with Clinical Decision Support, and the note that CDS impact may be assessed with an eCQM.
expert_raw_materials: Care-gap and quality reports, alert-override and alert-fatigue logs, patient-safety event reports, clinical practice guidelines, order-set and documentation-template drafts, EHR CDS knowledge artifacts, eCQM results for impact assessment.
usage_permissions: EHR production data are used under institutional policies and role-based access; guideline content is incorporated under publisher terms; CDS knowledge artifacts are governed by the institutional CDS governance committee.
task_input: CDS request from a clinical service or a detected care gap or alerting problem, with supporting guideline evidence and baseline workflow data.
professional_operations: Review the care gap or safety event and the evidence base; convene multidisciplinary review (clinicians, informatics, IT, quality); select the intervention format using the CDS Five Rights model; author or configure the rule in EHR tooling; test against representative and edge cases; implement with clinician education and change management; evaluate impact with an outcome or eCQM measure; monitor performance indicators continuously (alert override rates, drift); update or retire the intervention through the CDS governance committee.
expected_deliverable: Configured, tested, go-live CDS intervention with approval documentation, education record, and a monitoring or evaluation plan.
success_criteria: Improved process or outcome measure without new safety events; reduced alert overrides or documented rationale; scheduled governance review performed on time.
verification_approach: Override-rate and performance dashboards; eCQM or outcome measurement; chart audit of false-positive alerts; recurring CDS committee review of monitoring reports against baseline (PDSA-style comparison).
platform_dependencies: EHR CDS authoring environment (vendor or FHIR/CDS Hooks), analytics data warehouse, test patient or synthetic record sets, governance committee infrastructure.
blocking_risks: CDS configuration lives inside proprietary EHR vendor systems (institutional infrastructure, not portable software); alert-fatigue consequences of poorly tuned rules; regulatory uncertainty for self-developed adaptive CDS as documented by AMIA in the primary source.
expert_capability: Clinical informatics: workflow and knowledge management, CDS design and evaluation methods, clinical governance, EHR build competence.
cross_domain_overlap: Shares the evaluation step with med_inform_wf02 (eCQM lifecycle measures impact) - distinct because CDS changes clinician behavior while eCQM builds the measuring instrument. Adjacent to clinical_diagnostics and therapeutic_oncology workflows from the med_a round, which consume CDS rather than building it.

source_reference: PRIMARY: IHE IT Infrastructure Technical Framework Volume 1, Section 10, Cross-Enterprise Document Sharing (XDS.b), Final Text Revision 20.2, November 11 2025, fetched at https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/TF/Volume1/ch-10.html - documents the complete document sharing workflow: Document Source submits documents and metadata via Provide and Register Document Set-b (ITI-41), the Repository registers them with the Registry (ITI-42) with metadata validation, Consumers query via Registry Stored Query (ITI-18) and retrieve via Retrieve Document Set (ITI-43), patient identity feed (ITI-8 or 44), required groupings with Consistent Time and ATNA audit trail, affinity domain policies and metadata vocabulary, document lifecycle (approved, deprecated, replacement RPLC, addendum APND, transformation XFRM). workflow_title: Notifiable disease case surveillance: mandatory case reporting, case investigation, and national case notification through NNDSS
occupation_scope: Public health surveillance officer; Health department epidemiologist; Public health informatician
workflow_summary: Jurisdictional health departments receive legally mandated reports of diagnosed reportable conditions from providers, hospitals, and laboratories (via eCR and ELR), conduct case investigations to collect clinical and epidemiologic details and initiate control actions, then send de-identified case notifications for national notifiable conditions to CDC NNDSS, which validates, processes, and provisions the data to national disease programs.
source_reference: PRIMARY: CDC NNDSS (https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/conducting.html, fetched): documents the two-component case surveillance process - mandatory case reporting steps (diagnosis/confirmation reported to the health department; health department uses data for outbreak control, treatment assurance, and preventive care for exposed persons) and voluntary case notification steps (de-identified data sent to CDC; the NNDSS team receives, secures, processes, and provides data to disease-specific CDC programs), plus the methods eCR, ELR, NEDSS/NBS investigation-workflow systems, METS message validation, and MVPS validation/processing; SUPPORTING: CDC (https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/index.html, fetched): reportable-vs-notifiable distinction, about 120 notifiable conditions, about 3,000 health departments and 2.7M cases/year, CSTE and CDC set the national list, and CDC notification case records contain no personally identifiable information; CSTE/CDC case definitions repository (https://ndc.services.cdc.gov/, cited by the fetched CDC Field Epidemiology Manual chapter at https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/field-investigation.html).
expert_raw_materials: eCR and ELR messages; jurisdictional surveillance system records (NEDSS Base System or compatible); CSTE/CDC condition-specific case definitions; case investigation forms, interview notes, and laboratory results; state reportable-condition schedules and the annual NNDSS notifiable list; HL7 case notification messages validated through METS.
usage_permissions: Surveillance records are held and worked under state/local public health legal authority; national case notifications are de-identified and centrally provisioned by CDC NNDSS; CSTE/CDC case definitions are public documents in the ndc.services.cdc.gov repository; METS and MVPS services are restricted to jurisdictional users.
task_input: Reportable-condition reports (eCR/ELR) and lab/clinical results; the applicable CSTE/CDC case definition; the jurisdiction's reportable-condition list and investigation procedures.
professional_operations: Receive and triage eCR/ELR and provider reports against the case definition; open an investigation record in the jurisdictional system; collect demographic, clinical, epidemiologic, and exposure details; classify the case per case-definition criteria; initiate control actions (treatment follow-up, contact notification, prophylaxis, source control); validate and transmit de-identified notification for notifiable conditions to CDC via METS/MVPS; respond to CDC program queries and maintain data quality.
expected_deliverable: Completed case investigation records; de-identified case notifications submitted to NNDSS; documented disease-control actions; ad hoc jurisdictional reports and data extracts.
success_criteria: Complete, timely notifications accepted by MVPS; case classification matching CSTE/CDC case definition criteria; control actions initiated per protocol; no backlog of unprocessed reports.
verification_approach: METS message validation before transmission; MVPS portal data-quality review by jurisdictions; audit against case definition criteria; peer review within the health department program.
platform_dependencies: Jurisdictional surveillance information system (NEDSS Base System or NEDSS-compatible), eCR/EHR and ELR interfaces, METS and MVPS (CDC-hosted services), HL7 messaging, ndc.services.cdc.gov case definition repository.
blocking_risks: The workflow runs inside institutional public health systems (jurisdictional surveillance systems and CDC-hosted message services) with no portable equivalent; state-law variation in reporting requirements; identifiable case data cannot leave jurisdictional control, so automation must be embedded in health department environments; eCR/MMG onboarding requires CDC coordination.
expert_capability: Applied epidemiology with disease-specific investigation protocols, public health informatics (HL7/eCR/MMG message mapping), and command of state reporting laws and case definitions.
cross_domain_overlap: Feeds med_pubhealth_wf02 (outbreak investigations draw on case-level line listings) - distinct because wf01 is the routine case-level reporting-to-notification supply chain and wf02 is the episodic field response; touches clinical_informatics via eCR/EHR interfaces - distinct because clinical_informatics builds and operates the sending EHR systems while public health operates the receiving surveillance workflow.
granularity_check: Correct granularity: a bounded recurring per-case/per-batch workflow, not a career and not a single micro-action.
pending_confirmation: No critical gaps. Optional: confirm current MMG onboarding and eCR readiness thresholds with the NNDSS onboarding team (edx@cdc.gov).
data_usage_authorization: Case reporting by providers, hospitals, and laboratories is mandatory under state and local disease-reporting laws; notification to CDC is voluntary under CSTE/CDC agreements and CDC notification records contain no personally identifiable information (CDC NNDSS: https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/index.html). privacy_considerations: Case-level records are personally identifiable at the jurisdictional level and are protected under state disease-reporting laws; CDC notification records are de-identified (https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/index.html). US federal de-identification benchmarks for any shared analytic extracts follow the HIPAA Safe Harbor or expert determination standards of 45 CFR 164.514 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.514).

workflow_title: Epidemiologic field investigation of an outbreak (CDC 10-step method: confirm, characterize, control, communicate)
occupation_scope: Field epidemiologist; Health department epidemiologist
workflow_summary: After official authorization, a public health team confirms the diagnosis, verifies that an outbreak exists against expected baselines, builds a case definition and line listing, characterizes cases in time, place, and person, considers immediate control measures, develops and tests hypotheses, plans systematic studies, implements and evaluates control and prevention measures, and communicates findings through briefings and written reports.
source_reference: PRIMARY: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual, Ch. 3 Conducting a Field Investigation (King, Bensyl, Goodman, Rasmussen; https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/field-investigation.html, fetched): documents the complete 10-step field investigation workflow, including the three-element case definition (condition, period, setting), line listing, epidemic-curve construction at one-fourth to one-third of the incubation period, spot maps and denominators, source-directed versus susceptible-directed control measures, hypothesis testing with cohort/case-control studies and Bradford Hill considerations, active surveillance to evaluate control measures, and the communications plan ending in a preliminary written report and oral briefing to the requesting authority before leaving the field, with MMWR brief reports for rapid dissemination; discussion includes state legal privacy obligations for case information; SUPPORTING: CDC NNDSS case definitions repository (https://ndc.services.cdc.gov/, cited directly by this chapter) for the standard case definitions used in counting cases.
expert_raw_materials: Line listings; structured questionnaires (e.g., the CDC National Hypothesis Generating Questionnaire); laboratory results and strain typing; medical and institutional records; denominator counts (e.g., total event attendees); surveillance baselines; epidemic curves, spot maps, and other descriptive graphics; communications plans and briefing materials.
usage_permissions: Investigation data are collected under state/local public health legal authority following a formal invitation from an authorized official; laboratory work is coordinated with designated laboratories; questionnaire and case-definition tools are standard CDC instruments.
task_input: Notification of a suspected outbreak or cluster plus a formal invitation/authorization from the requesting authority.
professional_operations: 1 Prepare for field work (authorization, roles, laboratory coordination, PPE); 2 Confirm the diagnosis (interviews, exams, records, lab results; rule out pseudoepidemics); 3 Determine the existence of an outbreak (compare observed with expected counts/rates over a comparator timeframe); 4 Identify and count cases (case definition, active case finding, line listing); 5 Tabulate and orient data by time, place, and person (epidemic curves, spot maps, denominators); 6 Consider whether control measures can be implemented now; 7 Develop and test hypotheses (structured interviews, analytic studies, Bradford Hill considerations); 8 Plan one or more systematic studies; 9 Implement and evaluate control and prevention measures with concurrent active surveillance; 10 Communicate findings (communications plan, designated spokesperson, preliminary written report and oral briefing, final report, brief report for MMWR-type bulletins).
expected_deliverable: Line listing and descriptive epidemiologic products; preliminary written report and oral briefing to the requesting authority; recommendations for control; evaluation of control measures; final written report and possibly a brief report for a public health bulletin.
success_criteria: Outbreak confirmed or refuted on documented evidence; control measures implemented and shown by active surveillance to reduce or stop new cases; requesting authority receives the preliminary report and briefing before the team leaves the field.
verification_approach: Peer review by state/national colleagues; comparison of post-control case incidence via active surveillance; verification of case counts against laboratory results; requesting-authority review of the written report.
platform_dependencies: Line-listing and statistical software (spreadsheets, R or equivalent), mapping/GIS or simple plotting tools, laboratory information channels, secure communication for PII, and no specialized hardware.
blocking_risks: Substantial parts are inherently field-person work (interviews, site visits, briefings) that software cannot perform; access to identifiable case and exposure data is restricted by state law; laboratory confirmation and institutional EHR access depend on partnerships; readiness depends on trained field epidemiology staff.
expert_capability: Applied field epidemiology capability as taught in CDC EIS courses: descriptive and analytic epidemiology under time pressure, case-definition judgment, and public health communication.
cross_domain_overlap: Relies on case identification from med_pubhealth_wf01 (routine case surveillance builds the baseline and initial line listing) - distinct because wf01 is the routine case-level supply chain and wf02 is the episodic acute response; analytic study design within investigations is adjacent to clinical_trials observational study work - distinct because this is an urgent public health response under health authority, not regulated clinical research.
granularity_check: Correct granularity: an episodic but recurring, bounded professional workflow with published steps, not a career or micro-action.
pending_confirmation: No critical gaps. Optional: confirm current practice details (case-definition revision and control-measure timing) with a jurisdiction's state epidemiologist.
data_usage_authorization: Field investigation data collection operates under state/local public health legal authority, with a formal invitation from an authorized official required before assistance begins (https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/field-investigation.html); reported case data flow through the mandatory state-level reporting system documented by CDC NNDSS (https://www.cdc.gov/nndss/what-is-case-surveillance/index.html).
privacy_considerations: Investigation line listings contain personally identifiable information; the manual directs investigators to know applicable local, state, and federal privacy laws when collecting information from affected persons and their contacts (https://www.cdc.gov/field-epi-manual/php/chapters/field-investigation.html); US de-identification benchmarks follow 45 CFR 164.514 Safe Harbor or expert determination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.514).
research_ethics: Outbreak response is public health practice under legal authority, generally distinct from research; any systematic data collection or study added for publication in an investigation falls under the Common Rule research determination and IRB criteria of 45 CFR 46.111, including privacy safeguards and risk minimization (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.111). Under 45 CFR 46.102(l)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.102), public health surveillance activities conducted by a public health authority - including outbreak field investigations - are deemed not to be research when limited to detecting, monitoring, and investigating public health signals, outbreaks, and conditions of public health importance.

workflow_title: Daily syndromic surveillance monitoring and aberration investigation on the NSSP BioSense Platform (ESSENCE)
occupation_scope: Syndromic surveillance analyst; Health department epidemiologist
workflow_summary: Jurisdictional analysts access the NSSP BioSense Platform daily, review near real-time de-identified emergency department data (chief complaints, diagnosis codes, patient characteristics, location) for counts above expected baselines, run syndrome queries in the ESSENCE tool, investigate signals for outbreak plausibility, and communicate or escalate actionable findings - an early warning layer that precedes confirmed-disease reporting.
source_reference: PRIMARY: CDC NSSP About (For Public Health) (https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/index.html, fetched): documents the syndromic surveillance operation - de-identified facility data including chief complaint, diagnosis codes, patient characteristics, and location flow through health departments/HIEs into the CDC-hosted BioSense Platform where public health practitioners conduct surveillance activities to detect unusual levels of illness and determine whether a response is needed; lists integrated data sources (ED data, laboratory, mortality, DoD/VA, weather, air quality) and scale (7,500+ facilities, 85% of US EDs, 10.2M messages/day, data within 24 hours); SUPPORTING: CDC Syndromic Surveillance for New Users (https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/how-we-conduct-syndromic-surveillance.html, fetched): platform access is governed by jurisdictional site administrators, and ESSENCE is defined as the secure web-based tool that operationalizes the public health surveillance workflow, allowing analysts to collaborate, investigate changes in trends, and analyze, visualize, and share data; CDC MMWR overview of syndromic surveillance (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/su5301a3.htm, fetched): aberration-detection methods compare day-to-day and day-and-place variability against an expected baseline, response protocols need documented procedures and staff, diagnostic confirmation is a paramount alert-investigation step, and (as of 2004) signal-detection methods were not yet standardized.
expert_raw_materials: ED chief-complaint free text and coded fields; diagnosis codes; patient demographic and location fields; daily syndrome counts; ESSENCE queries, dashboards, and alert settings; data quality reports; baseline thresholds adjusted for seasonality and facility participation.
usage_permissions: BioSense Platform accounts are issued through jurisdictional site administrators who review data-access requests; platform data are de-identified; NSSP Community of Practice and knowledge repository resources support authorized users.
task_input: Daily refreshed BioSense Platform data plus situational requests (mass gatherings, disasters, respiratory season monitoring).
professional_operations: Maintain platform access through the site administrator; define categorical syndrome subsets and query library for the jurisdiction; review dashboards and alerts on a daily schedule; run ESSENCE queries against expected baselines to detect aberrations; investigate signals (clustering by location, severe symptoms, unexplained deaths, simultaneous multi-source alerts); pursue diagnostic confirmation where possible; document dispositions and communicate or escalate findings to investigation teams, and adjust syndrome definitions as disease knowledge evolves.
expected_deliverable: Daily situational awareness products; investigated and dispositioned alert records; event-related syndromic summaries; periodic reports of trends; documentation of syndrome definitions used.
success_criteria: Aberrations are detected in near real-time (data within 24 hours of visits); alerts are triaged and dispositioned with documented rationale; detected signals contribute to earlier investigation or response; monitoring continuity documented across analysts.
verification_approach: Corroboration of signals with other data sources (case reports, laboratories); diagnostic confirmation as part of alert investigation (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/su5301a3.htm); data quality review via platform reports; community of practice peer review of queries and definitions.
platform_dependencies: NSSP BioSense Platform (CDC-hosted cloud system) and the ESSENCE web application; jurisdictional data feed arrangements through health departments or HIEs; site-administrator account governance.
blocking_risks: The platform and ESSENCE are government-hosted services with jurisdiction-governed access and no self-host path, so the workflow cannot be reproduced outside official access; low positive predictive value of individual signals places the analytic burden on trained staff; alert thresholds remain jurisdiction-tuned rather than standardized; free-text coding quality varies by facility.
expert_capability: Syndromic surveillance methods training (e.g., CSTE introductory methodology courses linked from https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/how-we-conduct-syndromic-surveillance.html), time-series/aberration-detection literacy, and disease-epidemiology judgment.
cross_domain_overlap: Complements med_pubhealth_wf01 (case-based surveillance) and med_pubhealth_wf02 (outbreak investigation triggered by signals) - distinct because detection uses pre-diagnostic ED data in near real-time rather than confirmed case reports and laboratory follow-up; adjacent to clinical_informatics data feeds - distinct because informatics operates the sending EHR/eCR systems and public health operates the detection workflow.
granularity_check: Correct granularity: a bounded recurring daily workflow owned by a defined analyst role, not a career or micro-action.
pending_confirmation: No critical gaps. Optional: confirm current daily-monitoring SOP specifics (alert review cadence and disposition standards) with the NSSP CoP/OPHDST (nssp@cdc.gov).
data_usage_authorization: NSSP operates as a federal-state data-sharing program: participating facilities send de-identified syndromic data to state/local health departments and HIEs, which contribute to the CDC-hosted BioSense Platform for authorized public health surveillance (https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/index.html), and platform access is granted through jurisdictional site administrators (https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/how-we-conduct-syndromic-surveillance.html).
privacy_considerations: Syndromic records are de-identified before submission to health departments and the BioSense Platform per the NSSP data flow (https://www.cdc.gov/nssp/php/about/index.html); small-count disclosures still require statistical disclosure control, and the US de-identification benchmark is 45 CFR 164.514 Safe Harbor or expert determination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.514).
research_ethics: Syndromic surveillance is public health practice; the MMWR overview stresses that it does not replace traditional surveillance or physician reporting of unusual cases (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/su5301a3.htm); any research use of platform data follows the Common Rule research determination and IRB criteria of 45 CFR 46.111 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.111). Under 45 CFR 46.102(l)(2) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.102), public health surveillance conducted or authorized by a public health authority - including syndromic surveillance - is deemed not to be research when limited to detecting, monitoring, and investigating public health signals, outbreaks, and conditions of public health importance.
reproducibility_assessment: Platform-level tools and training make day-to-day query and visualization practice reproducible, but the MMWR overview documents that signal-detection methods and response protocols were historically not standardized across jurisdictions (https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/su5301a3.htm), so alert thresholds and syndrome definitions remain jurisdiction-specific rather than a single auditable standard.

workflow_title: BRFSS annual prevalence estimation: weighted analysis of the complex-survey public-use data file
occupation_scope: Public health data analyst; Health department epidemiologist (BRFSS coordinator)
workflow_summary: Each year, public health analysts obtain the BRFSS combined landline/cell public-use file, prepare variables with the codebook and calculated-variable documentation, apply the raked complex-sampling weights to the survey design, and compute state-level prevalence estimates of health risk behaviors with design-based variance estimation for reports, policy monitoring, and comparisons across post-2011 years.
source_reference: PRIMARY: CDC 2024 BRFSS Survey Data and Documentation (https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/annual_2024.html, fetched): documents the annual data-release workflow - the combined landline and cell phone dataset (457,670 records; 49 states plus DC, Guam, Puerto Rico, US Virgin Islands), raking weighting methodology in place since 2011 with the cell-phone frame, the codebook, calculated-variables documentation, variable layout, weighting/format resources, and the data quality report with response rates; states no data are not comparable to pre-2011 years; notes 2024 files were modified to comply with executive orders with possible missing-value inconsistencies; SUPPORTING: Complex Sampling Weights and Preparing Module Data for Analysis guidance (2024, https://www.cdc.gov/brfss/annual_data/2024/pdf/Complex-Sampling-Weights-and-Preparing-Module-Data-for-Analysis-2024-508.pdf - cited by the primary page; PDF not parsed in this round - the primary page records that it explains the need for complex sampling weights and instructions for preparing a module data set for analysis).
expert_raw_materials: BRFSS LLCP ASCII or SAS-transport public-use file; annual codebook; variable layout; calculated-variable documentation; complex-sampling-weights guidance; data quality report; optional module data files.
usage_permissions: Public-use data files and documentation are freely downloadable for analysis; respondent-level identifying data remain with state survey operations; the public-use files are de-identified.
task_input: BRFSS annual public-use data plus an analytic request (target indicators, geographic units, and population subgroups).
professional_operations: Download the data file, codebook, and variable layout; read and validate the fixed-position data; map variables and recode to analytic measures; build derived/calculated variables per documentation; declare the complex survey design with the raked weight (_LLCPWT) and strata; compute weighted prevalence and design-based confidence intervals for target indicators and subgroups; apply post-2011 comparability rules when trending across years; produce tables, maps, and reports with a methodology note.
expected_deliverable: Weighted prevalence estimates and design-based confidence intervals in tabular/report form; methodology documentation; monitoring briefs or public dashboards for health policy audiences.
success_criteria: Estimates reproduce CDC published BRFSS prevalence tables within rounding; standard errors reflect the complex design; trend statements respect the pre-2011 comparability boundary documented by CDC.
verification_approach: Replication against CDC published annual prevalence tables; data quality report review (response rates, coverage); state BRFSS coordinator review; independent code review of the weighting and recode logic.
platform_dependencies: Statistical software supporting complex survey designs (R survey package, SAS/SUDAAN, or Stata) on any OS; the ASCII/XPT public-use formats import on Linux through open packages; no proprietary runtime is strictly required.
blocking_risks: The 2024 weighting-formula detail is published as PDF documentation that must be read carefully to replicate CDC weights; executive-order-driven 2024 data modifications create missing-value inconsistencies noted by CDC; misuse of weights (unweighted analysis, ignoring design effects) silently invalidates estimates, so analyst training is the main gate.

workflow_title: Clinical trial site monitoring visits with source data verification (SDV)
occupation_scope: Clinical research associate (CRA) / clinical monitor; sponsor clinical operations and GCP quality assurance staff
workflow_summary: The sponsor's clinical monitor visits investigational sites on a planned schedule to verify that the study proceeds per protocol, GCP, and applicable regulations, compares source documents against case report form data (SDV), manages findings and queries, and documents the whole trail in monitoring reports from initiation through site close-out.
source_reference: PRIMARY: 21 CFR 312.56, Review of ongoing investigations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/312.56, fetched/read): the sponsor SHALL monitor the progress of all clinical investigations under its IND, secure compliance or discontinue an investigator on discovering noncompliance, and act on unreasonable and significant risk within 5 working days. SUPPORTING: 21 CFR 312.50, General responsibilities of sponsors (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/312.50, fetched/read): sponsor duties include ensuring proper monitoring of the investigation; FDA guidance 'Electronic Source Data in Clinical Investigations' (Sept 2013, docket FDA-2010-D-0643, https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/electronic-source-data-clinical-investigations, fetched/read): authorized source data originators, data element identifiers that facilitate audit-trail examination, and manual or electronic capture of source data into the eCRF - the objects SDV inspects; FDA guidance 'A Risk-Based Approach to Monitoring' (Aug 2013, docket FDA-2011-D-0597, https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/oversight-clinical-investigations-risk-based-approach-monitoring, fetched/read): monitoring as sponsor oversight focused on critical data and processes; GCDMP chapter 'Electronic Data Capture - Study Conduct, Maintenance and Closeout' (https://www.jscdm.org/article/id/31/, fetched/read, doi 10.47912/jscdm.31): quotes ICH E6(R2) sections 5.0/5.5 on sponsor oversight and source data, and records that SDV backlogs erode EDC value. The full ICH E6(R3) text was not HTML-accessible at research time (ich.org/EMA blocked), so its monitoring sections are cited only as referenced by fetched pages.
expert_raw_materials: Trial master file (TMF): monitoring plan, Form FDA-1572, delegation of authority log, IRB/IEC approvals; source documents (paper or electronic medical charts, lab reports, signed informed-consent forms); eCRF/EDC records with audit trails; monitoring visit logs and reports; correspondence with investigator; drug/device accountability records; SAE reconciliation lists
usage_permissions: Monitoring is a sponsor duty under 21 CFR 312.50 and 312.56 exercised per the study monitoring plan; site access to identifiable records requires site/IRB authorization and HIPAA-compliant disclosure basis (45 CFR 164.512(i) individual authorization or IRB waiver); monitors act under confidentiality agreements; TMF access governed by sponsor document-management permissions
task_input: Activated site: qualified investigator, executed 1572, IRB-approved protocol and amendments, enrolled subjects with eCRF data and source records, monitoring plan with visit schedule, safety and drug-accountability records
professional_operations: 1) Pre-study assessment and site selection; 2) site initiation visit (training, IRB approval verification, supplies, facility checks); 3) follow the monitoring calendar through interim monitoring visits; 4) verify signed informed consent exists for each enrolled subject and protocol compliance; 5) source data verification against eCRF for accuracy and completeness; 6) drug/device accountability and safety-reporting checks; 7) record findings, open queries and corrective actions with due dates; 8) write the monitoring visit report and escalate per risk thresholds; 9) close-out visit (finding resolution, archiving completeness, drug return, records retention)
expected_deliverable: Monitoring visit reports filed in the TMF; resolved queries with documented deviations; corrective and preventive action records; reconciled safety and drug-accountability logs; site close-out report
success_criteria: No unresolved critical findings at database lock; SDV coverage meets the monitoring plan; query resolution before lock per med_trials_wf02 gates; visit reports filed on schedule; protocol-deviation trends within acceptable limits across sites
verification_approach: Sponsor GCP quality assurance audits sample TMF/monitoring reports against SOPs; FDA BIMO inspections (21 CFR 312.68) review the same trail; CRO/sponsor monitoring management reviews reports per SOP; database-lock data-cleaning reports confirm query resolution
platform_dependencies: CTMS for visit scheduling and reporting; validated EDC with audit trail (21 CFR Part 11); eTMF/document management; electronic source access or remote monitoring tooling where EMRs are electronic; institutional site credentials; travel logistics
blocking_risks: Site access is governed by health-system policies, IRBs, and consent - an external agent cannot self-provision; SDV against heterogeneous EMR systems without standard APIs; CTMS/eTMF/EDC suites are commercial SaaS (portions replaceable by open EDC/CTMS such as OpenClinica but re-validation is costly); ICH E6(R3) procedural text is PDF-only on blocked hosts
expert_capability: GCP-credentialed CRA: protocol and regulatory fluency, source-data verification technique, risk escalation judgment, site training and corrective-action communication
cross_domain_overlap: Overlaps med_trials_wf02 (SDV-verified eCRFs feed data cleaning; distinct: wf02 owns the database to lock), med_trials_wf04 (risk-based strategy allocates visit frequency and triggers; distinct: wf04 designs where eyes go, wf01 puts eyes on site), and general audit workflows in other domains (legal/regulatory; distinct: clinical GCP compliance); biostatistics boundary: statistical monitoring designs belong to statistics, not this workflow
granularity_check: Right granularity: a bounded recurring per-study/per-site operational workflow from pre-study to close-out visit, neither a career nor a micro-action
pending_confirmation: Confirm with a GCP QA lead or ACRP-certified CRA that the reconstructed visit sequence (pre-study, initiation, interim monitoring with SDV, close-out) matches ICH E6(R3) Annex 1 monitoring provisions, whose full text was not HTML-accessible at research time (EMA/ich.org blocked or PDF-only); also confirm that SDV coverage follows the sponsor's monitoring plan rather than any fixed regulatory minimum.
data_usage_authorization: Sponsor monitoring duty mandated by 21 CFR 312.56(a) and 312.50 under the IND; access to identifiable subject data at sites is authorized under HIPAA 45 CFR 164.512(i) (individual authorization or IRB waiver) with minimum-necessary limits per 45 CFR 164.514(d); electronic records inspected must meet 21 CFR Part 11 controls (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/part-11); IND records retention per 21 CFR 312.57
privacy_considerations: Monitors handle subject-identifiable records; disclosure bases are HIPAA individual authorization or an IRB-approved waiver (45 CFR 164.512(i), https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.512), with access limited to the minimum necessary (45 CFR 164.514(d), https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/164.514); non-US jurisdictions apply their own rules (e.g., EU GDPR Article 89 research derogations in member-state law)
research_ethics: Monitoring protects enrolled subjects within an IRB-approved protocol: oversight and consent per 45 CFR 46.111, 46.116, and 46.117 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/45/46.111); monitors must not break blinding or bias study conduct; interim safety-only data review by independent committees follows the FDA Data Monitoring Committees guidance (March 2006, docket FDA-2001-D-0219, https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/establishment-and-operation-clinical-trial-data-monitoring-committees, fetched/read)
reproducibility_assessment: SOPs and a written monitoring plan make who/what/where/when of SDV reconstructable; monitoring reports plus eCRF and source-system audit trails form a complete auditable chain reviewable in FDA BIMO inspections; the documented trail is reproducible, the human chart-abstraction judgment is not
primary_claim: 21 CFR 312.56 requires the sponsor to monitor the progress of all clinical investigations under its IND (a), to secure compliance or discontinue investigators upon noncompliance (b), and to discontinue investigations posing unreasonable and significant risk within 5 working days (d), establishing the sponsor monitoring duty that site monitoring visits operationalize, without enumerating the visit-level procedure itself.

SUPPORTING: SCDM GCDMP hub (https://scdm.org/gcdmp/, fetched/read): GCDMP as global reference/benchmark with lifecycle chapters (data collection instruments, data management plan, edit checks, EDC selection and conduct); GCDMP Risk-Based Clinical Data Management chapter (https://www.jscdm.org/article/id/524/, fetched/read, doi 10.47912/jscdm.524): risk-based extension with KRIs and QTLs; 21 CFR 11.10 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/11.10, fetched/read): closed-system controls the database must satisfy (validation, audit trails, authority checks); FDA 'Electronic Source Data in Clinical Investigations' guidance (Sept 2013, docket FDA-2010-D-0643, page fetched/read): traceability from electronic source to regulatory submission.
expert_raw_materials: EDC database with eCRF data and audit trail; edit-check specifications; data management plan and CRF completion guidelines; query logs and cycle-time reports; central-lab/ECG/eCOA vendor transfer files; SAE reconciliation lists; MedDRA and WHODrug dictionaries; TMF/eTMF documents
usage_permissions: Role-based database access per the data management plan and SOPs (limited-access control per 21 CFR 11.10(d)/(g)); EDC and CRO service licenses; sponsor data governance and records retention policies (21 CFR 312.57); electronic signature authority per 21 CFR Part 11 Subpart C
task_input: Protocol with schedule of assessments; build-complete EDC with edit checks; enrolled subjects generating data and queries; central lab and external data feeds; SDV findings from med_trials_wf01
professional_operations: 1) Oversee data entry and perform continuous data surveillance; 2) run edit checks and issue queries to sites; 3) track query resolution and cleaning per cycle-time metrics (visit-to-entry, query-generation-to-resolution); 4) perform trend analyses, work lists, and high-volume communications; 5) reconcile external data (labs, safety database); 6) support mid-study reviews and interim (DSMB) analyses with near-real-time data; 7) apply incremental/form locks (lock-as-you-go); 8) final source-document review and DM close-out tasks; 9) database lock with freeze, audit copies, and archival; 10) manage post-lock changes under controlled procedures

success_criteria: Query resolution and cycle-time metrics meet DMP targets; zero open critical queries at lock; audit trail intact per 21 CFR 11.10(e); lock decision documented with cross-functional sign-off; external data fully reconciled with eCRF
verification_approach: Independent DM quality-assurance second-pass review; sponsor audit of EDC per Part 11 controls; audit-trail and access-privilege checks per FDA CSUCI guidance; lock quality gates with statistics, medical, and data-management sign-off
platform_dependencies: Validated EDC with edit checks and audit trail (21 CFR Part 11/11.10); query management; external data import and loading; SDTM/SAS-ready dataset generation; eTMF filing; electronic signatures (21 CFR 11.100-11.300)
blocking_risks: Commercial EDC/SaaS dominates and open-source replacement (e.g., OpenClinica) still requires re-validation and integration; query triage and investigator responses involve clinical judgment not fully automatable; Part 11 validation cannot be delegated to an unvalidated agent; DSMB interim cuts need restricted access workflows
expert_capability: Certified clinical data manager applying GCDMP: study database lifecycle, ALCOA data integrity, edit-check design, query management, dictionary coding, and coordination with statistics, safety, and clinical teams
cross_domain_overlap: Receives SDV from med_trials_wf01 and provides KRI source data to med_trials_wf04 and analysis-ready data for med_trials_wf05 results; distinct because wf02 owns the study database lifecycle through lock; biostatistics boundary: DM produces clean data, statistics defines derivations and analyses

workflow_title: Serious adverse event assessment and expedited IND safety reporting
occupation_scope: Drug safety/pharmacovigilance professional; sponsor safety physician or coordinator; CRO PV associate; site research staff performing investigator reports
workflow_summary: Serious adverse events are assessed for seriousness, relatedness, and expectation against the investigator brochure, then reportable events are filed to FDA and notified to participating investigators within expedited statutory timelines, using FDA Form 3500A/CIOMS I and mandated follow-ups per 21 CFR 312.32.
source_reference: PRIMARY: 21 CFR 312.32, IND safety reporting (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/312.32, fetched/read; amended at 91 FR 60003): defines adverse event, serious, suspected adverse reaction, unexpected; requires sponsor review of all safety information from any source (b); reportable categories (c)(1)(i)-(iv); 15-calendar-day reporting (c)(1) and 7-calendar-day reporting for unexpected fatal or life-threatening suspected adverse reactions (c)(2); format requirements - FDA Form 3500A, CIOMS I for foreign reporting, narrative for pooled analyses, electronic format per FDA guidance, marked IND Safety Report to the CDER/CBER review division (c)(1)(v); follow-up investigation and Followup IND Safety Reports (d). SUPPORTING: 21 CFR 312.64 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/312.64, fetched/read): investigator must immediately report any serious adverse event to the sponsor with causality assessment - the intake leg of the chain; 21 CFR 312.50 (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/312.50, fetched/read): sponsor must promptly inform FDA and investigators of significant new risks. NOTE: the ICH E2A page at EMA (https://www.ema.europa.eu/en/ich-e2a-clinical-safety-data-management-definitions-and-standards-expedited-reporting) could not be fetched (unsupported content type on two attempts) and its definitions are not cited from parsed text.
expert_raw_materials: SAE reports from investigators per 312.64(b); source documents (discharge summaries, labs); current investigator brochure (IB); safety database case records; MedDRA coding dictionaries; protocol safety-reporting section and DSMB charter; FDA Form 3500A and CIOMS I templates; prior IND safety reports
usage_permissions: Sponsor holds the IND (21 CFR 312.30); safety reporting is mandatory under 21 CFR 312.32; electronic submissions through the FDA Electronic Submissions Gateway (ESG) per FDA guidance; safety-database access per company pharmacovigilance SOPs; MedDRA under MSSO subscription terms
task_input: Incoming SAE notifications from sites; new signals from literature, animal/in vitro studies, and other studies per 312.32(b); current IB and protocol safety definitions
professional_operations: 1) Triage and intake with complete data capture; 2) medical seriousness, causality, and expectedness assessment; 3) determine reportability under 312.32(c)(1)(i)-(iv); 4) code terms with MedDRA; 5) draft narrative with patient chronology and follow-up plan; 6) file FDA Form 3500A electronically within 15 or 7 calendar days; 7) notify all participating investigators; 8) update the IB/safety information as needed; 9) track follow-ups and file Followup IND Safety Reports (312.32(d)); 10) escalate to DSMB if protocol stopping rules engage
expected_deliverable: Timely IND safety reports to the FDA review division; investigator notifications on record; updated safety-database cases and IB; cumulative safety contributions to the annual report (21 CFR 312.33) and DSMB safety tables
success_criteria: Report filed within 15 calendar days of determination (7 for unexpected fatal/life-threatening); zero missed reportable events confirmed by SAE-source vs safety-database reconciliation; narrative completeness auditable; investigator notifications documented
verification_approach: Pharmacovigilance compliance audits (source-list vs safety-database reconciliation); FDA IND inspection review of safety files; timeliness KPIs with CAPAs; two-person verification of each regulatory package
platform_dependencies: Validated safety database (21 CFR Part 11); ESG gateway for electronic submissions; MedDRA; document management; 24/7 intake procedures; contingency channels for investigator notification
blocking_risks: Validated commercial PV databases (Argus/ArisGlobal-class) are institutional and open-source pharmacovigilance tooling is not a like-for-like validated replacement; ICH E2B(R3) exchange is open but FDA gateway integration is institutional; causality/expectedness are medical judgments; statutory deadlines leave no tolerance for automation failure
expert_capability: Drug-safety professional or medical reviewer with command of 21 CFR 312.32: severity/causality/expectedness assessment, MedDRA coding, narrative writing, deadline management, IB updating
cross_domain_overlap: Feeds med_trials_wf05 (ClinicalTrials.gov AE summary tables per 42 CFR 11.48(a)(4) derive from the safety database) and med_trials_wf02 (SAE reconciliation); distinct from postmarketing pharmacovigilance surveillance (public-health adjacent) because this is sponsor reporting under an IND; biostatistics boundary: DSMB analyses of accumulated safety data

pending_confirmation: No critical gaps. Optional: confirm current electronic submission mechanics (ESG and ICH E2B(R3) file formats) with an FDA electronic-submissions liaison or PV operations director - the ICH E2A page was unfetchable at research time.

workflow_summary: The responsible party determines applicability, registers the applicable clinical trial in the National Library of Medicine PRS, maintains the record through amendments, and submits structured results information (participant flow, baseline characteristics, outcome measures and analyses, adverse-event tables, protocol/SAP documents) within statutory deadlines under 42 CFR Part 11.

professional_operations: 1) Determine whether the trial is an applicable clinical trial (11.22) and identify the responsible party; 2) register before the deadline with 11.28 data elements and obtain the NCT number; 3) update the record during the trial (recruitment status, amendments); 4) at completion determine results obligation and deadline from the primary completion date (11.42); 5) assemble structured modules in PRS: participant flow, baseline, outcome analyses, AE tables (11.48(a)(1)-(4)); 6) upload protocol and SAP with redactions (11.48(a)(5)); 7) run quality review against an 11.48 checklist; 8) submit, requesting 11.54 waivers where eligible; 9) track corrections and maintain the disclosure compliance log
expected_deliverable: Complete registered record and results record publicly posted on ClinicalTrials.gov; internal disclosure compliance log (NCT numbers, submission dates, supporting evidence)
success_criteria: Registration posted before requirements deadlines; results certified and posted within 11.44 timing; no PRS validation errors left unresolved; public record complete against an 11.48 self-checklist; no notices of non-compliance
verification_approach: Independent second-reviewer QA against an 11.48 content checklist; periodic disclosure audits vs the registry; response tracking for NIH results QC comments; monitoring of Subpart E enforcement
platform_dependencies: ClinicalTrials.gov PRS web portal with organization account; document preparation and PDF-redaction tooling; eTMF storage of submission milestones; statistical outputs from the trial analysis platform
